title: Nsight sampled epoch-slice runbook: microbatch alignment
content:
Context and goal:

This is a working write-up of a short Nsight sampling campaign we ran to understand why tail latency and aggregate GPU efficiency diverge when using small microbatch sizes (1-4 tokens per microbatch) across our decoder stack. Previous traces hinted at repeated short kernels with large inter-kernel gaps; this run focuses on slicing request execution into short epoch windows to capture intermittent SM wake/sleep behavior and launch bursts.

Why this is different from prior recordings:
- Instead of recording a single long trace, we take many short, aligned samples ('epoch slices') anchored to the request lifecycle (request arrival, KV-prefetch, first-token, steady-state generation, last-token).
- Goal is to reveal periodic quiescence (SMs idle for tens of microseconds) and quantify whether gaps correlate with host->device copy windows, KV cache misses, or kernel launch serialization.

Environment and versions (repro):
- Model: rdx-6b-decoder-qat (fp16, fused attention kernels)
- Runtime binary: serving-runtime v0.58.1 (bundle-2026-04-27)
- Driver: NVIDIA 535.86
- CUDA: 12.2
- Nsight: nsys 2026.1, ncu 2026.1
- Hardware: A40x8 cluster (shared test slab), PCIe gen4 nodes with NVLink disabled for this slab

Sampling methodology:
1) Emit NVTX spans at these callsites in runtime: request_enqueue, prefetch_kv_start, prefetch_kv_end, kernel_launch_batch, first_token_emit, last_token_emit. We added short markers so traces can be aligned.
2) For each workload config (microbatch sizes = 1, 2, 4, 8; sequence lengths = 64, 128), perform 30 epoch slices. An epoch slice is a 50ms capture centered on first_token_emit (20ms before, 30ms after).
3) Use nsys in short-recording loop to minimize overhead from recording large traces: nsys profile --output=epoch_{i} --trace=nvtx,cuda,osrt --sample=cpu --duration=50ms --capture-range=nvtx --stop-on-exit -- python -u run_inference.py ...
4) Postprocess each epoch by extracting kernel launch timestamps, kernel durations, SM active percentages, and L2 utilization from ncu reports (ncu export) and nsight summaries.

Representative commands used:
- Recording: nsys profile --trace=nvtx,cuda --force-overwrite true --capture-range=nvtx --output epoch-001 -- python run_inference.py --config=mb1_s128
- Quick ncu: ncu -k sm__cycles_elapsed.avg,sm__inst_executed.avg,sm__active_warps.avg --target-processes=all --section 'Occupancy' --csv -o ncu_epoch_001 ncu_report

Key observations (executive summary):
1) Launch burst pattern: For microbatch=1, we consistently see 3–6 short (<150us) kernels launched in rapid succession on first-token path, then a quiescent gap of 40–110us before the steady-state generation kernels. The burst density and gap magnitude reduce as microbatch increases.
2) Low achieved occupancy during bursts: Many of the short kernels report SM active warps at 15–28%, with tensor core utilization near zero. Longer steady-state kernels hit higher tensor core utilization (30–48%) and SM active warps ~55–70%.
3) Host-driven serialization: NVTX alignment plus host-side traces show these gaps coincide with small host-side syscall spikes (sched_yield/epoll_wait wakeups) and memcpy launches. The ordering implies host thread scheduling contributes to serialization of kernel launches when per-token latency is small.
4) KV-prefetch impact: When KV cache miss rate > 15% (simulated via config), we see an extra 200–500us tail in prefetch window and additional small memcpy kernels; these amplify the post-burst gap.
5) Kernel launch overhead sensitivity: Enabling CUDA graph capture (where we recorded end-to-end generation kernels as a graph) collapsed the launch bursts into a single graph launch; this reduced inter-kernel gaps but introduced variability in early warmup when graph instantiation occurred (graph instantiation cost ~120–260us once per request when not cached).

Detailed slices and numbers (selected):
- Microbatch=1, seq=128 (median across 30 slices):
  - Burst: 5 short kernels, durations = [40us, 70us, 110us, 90us, 60us]
  - Gap (burst -> steady): 86us median
  - SM active warps in burst: 18%
  - SM active warps in steady: 62%
  - Token throughput (tokens/s): 8200

- Microbatch=4, seq=128 (median):
  - Burst: 2 short kernels durations = [110us, 210us]
  - Gap: 22us median
  - SM active warps in burst: 36%
  - SM active warps in steady: 68%
  - Token throughput (tokens/s): 16,400

Hypotheses and interpretation:
- At small microbatch sizes the runtime submits many small kernels for different operator fragments (e.g., pre/post transforms, attention split, post-softmax) synchronously from host threads. The overhead of many small host->driver submissions plus host scheduling jitter introduces idle windows where SMs could have been doing useful work if kernels had been fused or batched.
- CUDA graph capture compresses driver overhead but shifts cost to graph creation/instantiation and makes warmup worse when graphs are not already cached per model-shape. Graph caching reduces variance but requires us to manage per-shape graph eviction policy.
- KV-prefetch patterns that cause device-side memcpy churn amplify idle gaps; improving prefetch concurrency or moving to double-buffered copies can hide some of that latency.

Immediate mitigation experiments to run next:
- Experiment A (fusion-first): Build a microkernel that fuses the small ops for first-token path and run 30 epoch slices. Measure reduction in burst count and gap duration. Owner: Ethan. Target date: 2026-05-24.
- Experiment B (graph caching policy): Implement an LRU graph cache keyed on (model-id, seq-len, microbatch) and benchmark warmup costs vs steady-state. Owner: Priya. Target date: 2026-05-26.
- Experiment C (double-buffer prefetch): Modify KV prefetch to asynchronously issue two overlapping cudaMemcpyAsync windows and measure if gap reduces. Owner: Liam. Target date: 2026-05-25.

Longer-term ideas (design notes):
- Shift more orchestration to CUDA streams on-device: reduce host submission count by having a single host enqueuer that concatenates small kernels into a single stream-based pipeline on device.
- Adaptive microbatching: if measured inter-kernel gap > X us and per-token latency SLO allows, increase microbatch for that request to reduce driver overhead.
- Add per-route graph warmup during cold start: prebuild graphs for common shapes when a model is loaded into pool.

Trace artifacts and how to view them:
- Raw epoch traces are in the test slab under /traces/epoch-slices/ (confluence link: CONFLUENCE-1234 contains exact locations). Use Nsight Systems GUI to open epoch-00X.qdrep and filter NVTX spans 'first_token_emit' to align.
- NCU csv exports attached to GH-PR-4876 show aggregated occupancy tables per kernel. Look at sm__active_warps.avg and sm__inst_executed.avg to compute occupancy ratios used above.

Open questions / uncertainties:
- How much of the host-side syscall jitter is due to our Python harness vs Go runtime used in production? We tested in Python; need to re-run minimal C++ harness.
- When using NVLink-enabled nodes, does the increased PCIe peer bandwidth eliminate memcpy gaps or just shift them? Not tested here.

Notes to self / quick checklist before next run:
- Add a small histogram export of inter-launch gaps into stdout for each epoch run (dump JSON).
- Re-run sampling on a c++ binary to validate host scheduling hypothesis.
- Instrument graph cache hit/miss counters in runtime and log them into the trace NVTX metadata.

Appendix: quick command history used during session:
- build: bazel build //serving:runtime_bin --config=release -c opt
- record loop (bash): for i in {1..30}; do nsys profile --trace=nvtx,cuda --output epoch-${i} --duration=50ms -- python run_inference.py --shape mb1_s128; sleep 0.2; done
- ncu sample: ncu -o ncu_epoch_${i}.csv --csv --target-processes=all --section 'ComputeWorkloadAnalysis' --set full --launch-mode=system --n 1 ncu_report

Action items recap:
- Ethan: implement minimal fusion for first-token pipeline (due 2026-05-24)
- Priya: graph cache LRU prototype + perf run (due 2026-05-26)
- Liam: prototype double-buffered KV prefetch and sample runs (due 2026-05-25)
- Maya: re-run with c++ harness and add inter-launch gap histogram export (due 2026-05-22)

If useful we can convert this into a short slides deck for infra sync. This note intentionally keeps raw sample numbers and commands so infra can reproduce quickly.
